stories.headline: Avalanche Sign Cale Makar to Largest Contract in NHL History at $163.2 Million
stories.summary:
Colorado Avalanche defenseman Cale Makar agreed Friday to an eight-year, $163.2 million contract extension, making him the first player in NHL history to carry a $20 million annual cap hit and keeping him in Denver through 2035. The deal surpasses the previous high-water marks set this offseason by Leo Carlsson ($18 million) and Macklin Celebrini ($18.8 million), reshaping the financial landscape of the league overnight.

Makar, widely regarded as the NHL's premier defenseman, has won the Norris Trophy twice and been named a finalist six times in seven seasons. He also captured the Calder Trophy as rookie of the year and the Conn Smythe Trophy during Colorado's 2022 Stanley Cup championship run.

League analysts reacted with a mixture of awe and affirmation. ESPN analyst Kevin Weekes called Makar 'transformational,' while MSG Network's Cory Schneider said the contract reflects the rapidly evolving financial reality of the modern NHL. Minnesota's Quinn Hughes, the only defenseman considered Makar's peer, remains unsigned and could push the market higher still.

The extension cements Makar's legacy in Denver and puts him on a clear path to the Hockey Hall of Fame. With the Avalanche entering 2026-27 after a difficult offseason, retaining their franchise cornerstone is seen as the organization's most critical move of the summer.

stories.headline: Broncos Rout Vikings 34-6 in Preseason Finale at Empower Field
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos closed out the 2026 preseason with a dominant 34-6 victory over the Minnesota Vikings on Friday night at Empower Field at Mile High. The lopsided result capped a preseason in which quarterback Bo Nix drew consistent praise from teammates and coaching staff heading into his third NFL season.

The game served as the final audition for roster bubble players before Denver must trim its squad to the regular-season limit. The Broncos had previously struggled in a 33-13 loss to Green Bay in Week 2 of the preseason, making Friday's performance a needed confidence boost entering the regular season.

Defensive coordinator Vance Joseph and the coaching staff used the contest to evaluate backfield depth and secondary options, including the status of cornerback Riley Moss, who had left an earlier preseason game with a rib injury. The team made several roster transactions in the days leading up to the finale.

Denver's convincing margin of victory sets an optimistic tone as the franchise prepares for the regular season opener. With Nix described by teammates as 'playing out of his mind,' expectations around the Broncos' offense are elevated entering 2026-27.

stories.headline: Nuggets Shed Peyton Watson in Salary Cap Move, Continue Apron Maneuvering
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets traded forward Peyton Watson to the Cleveland Cavaliers as part of ongoing efforts to reduce payroll and create flexibility beneath the NBA's second apron threshold for the 2026-27 season. The move is the latest in a series of transactions aimed at reshaping the roster's financial structure without sacrificing core talent.

The second apron, a hard-cap mechanism designed to promote competitive balance, has significantly constrained the Nuggets' ability to retain depth and add talent this offseason. Team management opted not to pay Watson, whose development had been closely watched since he was drafted, choosing instead to prioritize cap room.

The trade opens additional options for Denver to pursue further moves before the regular season begins. Former Nuggets general manager Calvin Booth, who oversaw much of the team's roster construction during its championship era, is departing the Denver area entirely, with he and his wife listing their Cherry Hills Village home for $5.2 million.

stories.headline: Front Range Passenger Rail Board Votes to Put Sales Tax on November Ballot for Southern Rail Expansion
stories.summary:
The Front Range Passenger Rail District's Board of Directors voted 14-1 Friday to refer a new sales tax measure to November voters that would fund a southern extension of the Colorado Connector passenger rail line. The 0.333% tax — equivalent to 33 cents on every $100 spent — would add two daily trips between Denver's Union Station and Pueblo, with stops at Sterling Ranch, Littleton and Colorado Springs, while also adding a fourth daily trip to the northern segment reaching Fort Collins.

The Colorado Connector, already funded in part by RTD and CDOT, is set to begin linking Union Station to Westminster, Broomfield, Louisville, Boulder, Longmont, Loveland and Fort Collins through three daily trips starting in 2029. The southern extension would significantly broaden the network's reach into the state's second-largest population corridor. The tax would not apply to food, gasoline, residential utilities, prescription drugs or medical supplies.

Community leaders from across the region testified in support before the vote, including Larimer County Commissioner Kristin Stephens, who said states with robust rail networks have seen strong economic results. Boulder County Commissioner and board member Claire Levy framed the project as part of a broader statewide transit transformation that also includes expanded Bustang service and a potential Mountain Rail line to the Western Slope.

One dissenting voice came from former RTD director Natalie Menten of Jefferson County, who said she could not envision using the service. The measure now goes before Front Range voters in November, where it will face the challenge of winning approval across a politically diverse electorate spanning urban, suburban and rural communities.

stories.headline: Denver Man Charged With Felony Tampering After Sabotaging Front Range Water Infrastructure for Years
stories.summary:
Denver resident Fabrizio Lorenzin, 65, faces four felony charges after allegedly tampering with the Berthoud Pass Watershed Ditch system over a period of several years, diverting millions of dollars' worth of drinking water intended for Northglenn and Golden. The Colorado Attorney General's Office and the 14th District Attorney's Office announced the charges Friday, citing repeated sabotage of headgates and the theft of security cameras monitoring the remote ditch system.

Prosecutors allege Lorenzin's actions began in August 2019, when he forced open four headgates and diverted water valued at approximately $1.3 million. He allegedly struck again in 2022, causing $4.3 million in water losses, and returned in 2023 to damage another gate and steal trail cameras. Federal investigators with the EPA eventually planted cameras with Apple AirTags, which later pinged from inside Lorenzin's Denver home.

A search of Lorenzin's residence uncovered disassembled EPA cameras and a laptop containing images from other stolen devices. The laptop's search history revealed multiple queries related to sabotage of the Berthoud Pass system as well as trail cameras and headgates. Investigators had captured images of the same man with a distinctive backpack across multiple incidents before identifying Lorenzin.

Lorenzin faces one count of tampering with a public water system, two counts of felony theft, and one count of tampering with evidence. Attorney General Phil Weiser called protecting critical water infrastructure a 'core public safety mission.' Court records confirm Lorenzin has been arrested. No motive has been publicly disclosed.

stories.headline: Copper Mountain Roller Coaster Closed After Rider Suffers Life-Altering Injuries, State Investigating
stories.summary:
The Rocky Mountain Coaster at Copper Mountain ski resort has been closed since Aug. 17 following an incident in which Texas resident Nicola Parker was allegedly ejected from the ride, became tangled in her seatbelt and was dragged along the tracks. Her attorneys say Parker sustained a punctured and collapsed lung, a traumatic brain injury, and extensive cuts and abrasions across her body.

The Colorado Division of Oil and Public Safety, which regulates amusement park ride safety, is conducting an investigation. The state has instructed the ride's manufacturer to issue a safety bulletin and share it with other operators. A similar coaster at Purgatory Resort has also been closed pending the outcome of the probe.

Parker's law firm, Colorado-based Bloch Ongert, said she had her seatbelt properly fastened and followed all resort instructions, calling the incident 'horrific' and one that 'should have never occurred.' No lawsuit has been filed yet, as attorneys are waiting for the investigation to conclude before taking legal action.

Copper Mountain confirmed the closure and said it is working with state officials and the manufacturer to review the incident. Documentation related to the investigation will not be released publicly until it is complete. Copper Mountain is located west of Breckenridge in Summit County.

stories.headline: Bear Attacks Woman in Her 80s Inside Estes Park Home, Marking Seventh Human Attack This Year
stories.summary:
A bear broke into an Estes Park home early Thursday morning and attacked a woman in her 80s, scratching her across the abdomen and knocking her to the ground before escaping through the same first-floor window it used to enter. The woman sought immediate medical treatment, and Larimer County deputies found no bear in the surrounding area upon arrival. Colorado Parks and Wildlife is now seeking assistance from the USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service to locate the animal.

The attack is the seventh human bear attack in Colorado this year, which CPW has described as an 'unprecedented' conflict season. More than 6,000 bear sightings have been reported statewide — nearly double last year's figures — driven in large part by worsening drought conditions that have depleted natural food sources, forcing bears into populated areas in search of the roughly 20,000 daily calories they need before winter hibernation.

CPW reports heavy bear activity in the Estes Park area specifically, with multiple bears breaking into occupied homes and vehicles in recent days. Officers have set traps to remove bears posing an immediate public safety risk. The agency is urging residents to secure food and trash and to lock all windows, even on upper floors.

Colorado is also entering the hyperphagia season, a metabolic phase during which bears feed almost constantly to prepare for denning. Wildlife managers say bear conflict reports are expected to climb further in the weeks ahead and are asking the public to remain vigilant.

stories.headline: 4.25 Million Gallons of Raw Sewage Flow Into Arkansas River After Pueblo Pipe Failure
stories.summary:
A failed wastewater pipe in Pueblo released 4.25 million gallons of raw sewage into the Arkansas River beginning Wednesday, prompting state health warnings for farmers and recreators as far east as Las Animas to avoid contact with the water. The pipe, which had been repaired with concrete inside a stormwater discharge pipe, burst under pressure and was discovered and shut down Thursday. By Friday night, downstream water samples showed 'extremely high' levels of E. coli bacteria.

The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment advised people not to recreate in or use river water until testing confirms a return to normal levels, and warned that pets and livestock should also be kept away from the river. State agriculture and health officials are working with melon and produce farmers in the Lower Arkansas Valley — who depend on the river for irrigation — to find alternative water sources and conduct safety testing.

Water officials said the drought is compounding the crisis: low river flows eliminate the dilution effect that would normally help flush contaminants downstream more quickly. Most produce growers in the area rely on groundwater this season, offering some protection, but those using surface water from the Arkansas River face significant challenges.

No evidence has emerged of contamination in public drinking water systems downstream, as utilities were notified early enough to close their intakes. People using private wells or water supplies who suspect contamination are advised to contact CDPHE's Water Quality Control Division.

stories.headline: Wildfire Near Estes Park Prompts Mandatory Evacuations in Pinewood Springs and Blue Mountain
stories.summary:
The Moose Mountain Fire, burning between Estes Park and Lyons in Larimer County, prompted mandatory evacuation orders for residents of Pinewood Springs and Blue Mountain on Friday afternoon. The Larimer Emergency Telephone Authority issued the orders at 1:30 p.m. after the blaze was reported at approximately 1.5 acres in size, growing to between 1.5 and 2 acres by late afternoon as multiple fire agencies worked to build containment lines.

Mandatory evacuation orders were later lifted, but residents in the Pinewood Springs area remained under voluntary evacuation status as of Friday evening. Smoke from the fire was visible in the Lyons area, though Boulder County officials said there were no evacuations or road closures on their side of the county line as of Friday afternoon.

The fire comes during an extended period of drought and elevated fire danger across Colorado's Front Range foothills. The bear conflict crisis and this wildfire both underscore the ecological stress drought conditions are placing on the region heading into September.

Residents in affected areas were directed to text LCEVAC to 888777 for real-time updates and to visit nocoalert.org for evacuation maps. Denver7's northern Colorado reporter was on scene and relayed updates from local fire officials throughout the afternoon.

stories.headline: Five Points Community Debates Future of Welton Street Light Rail as Summer Suspension Continues
stories.summary:
Denver's Department of Transportation and Infrastructure and RTD held a virtual community meeting Thursday night to discuss the future of the light-rail line along Welton Street in the Five Points neighborhood, which has been suspended this summer for maintenance. Options under consideration range from upgrading the existing tracks for another 30 years to converting the corridor to bus service, pedestrian-friendly streetscaping or even relocating transit to an adjacent street entirely.

Some business owners and residents along Welton Street — historically the main corridor of Denver's Black community — say the suspension presents an opportunity to reimagine the street as a more vibrant, pedestrian-centered destination akin to Larimer Square. Complaints about the light-rail alignment include the narrow right-of-way, lack of tree canopy, and poor connectivity to the broader downtown and River North transit network.

An initial community survey of approximately 500 respondents in May prioritized shade, greenery, safe sidewalks and seating. Those who want transit to remain on Welton Street largely want improved stop quality and faster travel times. The study also examines a potential extension of the line to connect with the A Line, which runs from Union Station to Denver International Airport.

A final plan and decision are expected in spring 2027. Project manager Phoebe Gryzlo told participants the city does not want to see Welton Street become 'an empty, quiet corridor' and acknowledged that the process will involve competing community visions.

stories.headline: Michelin-Starred Beckon Team to Open New Neighborhood Bistro Holm in Former Table 6 Space
stories.summary:
Paired Hospitality, the Denver restaurant group behind Michelin-starred Beckon and Major Tom on Larimer Street, announced plans to open a new neighborhood bistro called Holm at 609 Corona St. — the space vacated last month by the long-running East Sixth Avenue restaurant Table 6. The 50-seat restaurant is expected to open in October.

Unlike Beckon's chef's tasting menu format, Holm is designed to offer a casual, 'hyperseasonal' menu suitable for weeknight dinners and special occasions alike. Dishes will include comfort-oriented fare such as brick chicken with poached fall vegetables and pork ragù with housemade pasta, alongside vegetable-forward plates using produce from the owners' farm in Lakewood.

Holm is the creation of husband-and-wife team Duncan and Allison Holmes, along with partners Josh Elson and Craig Lieberman. Duncan Holmes will serve as head chef. The name is a play on both 'home' and the couple's surname.

The opening marks continued expansion for Paired Hospitality even as Denver's restaurant industry faces broader headwinds. Beckon earned its first Michelin star in 2023 and has established the group as one of the city's most prominent fine-dining operators.

stories.headline: Bruz Beers to Close Denver's Bruz Off Fax Location, Plans New Golden Production Facility
stories.summary:
Bruz Beers, the Denver-based Belgian-style brewery, announced that its Bruz Off Fax taproom at 1495 York St. will close permanently on Sept. 24 when its lease expires. The closure will allow the company to concentrate its resources on building a new, larger production facility and taproom in Golden at a property it purchased in November 2025.

Co-founder and CEO Ryan Evans said the brewery simply outgrew the York Street location, which debuted in February 2020 — just before the COVID-19 pandemic forced the industry to pivot. The company plans to host a proper farewell event before closing day. The Golden project is expected to take a couple of years to complete.

Brewery fans will still have access to Bruz's original Midtown location at 1675 W. 67th Ave. in Denver, which will remain open throughout the transition. Evans credited a loyal neighborhood fanbase and the brewery's niche focus on Belgian ales — along with diversification into wine, cider and imported Belgian beers — for helping the company grow despite a broader slump in the craft beer industry.

Bruz Beers also noted that ongoing Colfax Avenue Bus Rapid Transit construction near the Off Fax location, while a nuisance for other nearby businesses, did not cause dramatic drops in visitation. The Golden expansion represents the company's first owned real estate.

weather.notable: Nearly 6 degrees above the average high for this time of year.

joke.joke: In terms of instant relief, canceling plans is like heroin.

topStory.headline: Trump's Shifting Rhetoric on Iran War Marked by Contradictions, Stalled Negotiations
topStory.summary:
President Trump has spent the past six months attempting to shape public perception of the ongoing conflict with Iran, according to reporting from the Los Angeles Times, characterizing the war's resolution as imminent even as negotiations have repeatedly stalled. Throughout that period, Trump has swung between conciliatory and confrontational postures, at times describing Iran's current leadership as more reasonable than their predecessors, only to later refer to the same officials as "sick individuals."

The inconsistency in Trump's public statements has extended to contradictions with his own Cabinet, with discrepancies emerging not only within the same week but on the same day in some instances. Axios documented the shifting positions through six specific quotes that illustrate the evolution — and reversal — of the administration's stated goals for the conflict.

The broader context is one of prolonged diplomatic uncertainty, with Trump repeatedly signaling that a deal was within reach while substantive progress has remained elusive. The pattern reflects a tension between the administration's desire to project strength and the operational and diplomatic complexity of winding down a military engagement with Iran.

The disconnect between the White House's public messaging and the realities on the ground has raised questions among analysts and lawmakers about the administration's defined objectives and exit strategy. How the administration reconciles its internal divisions and communicates a coherent endgame to both domestic and international audiences is expected to remain a central issue in the weeks ahead.
